node.label: Luise White
node.date_label: The Comforts of Home (1990) · Speaking with Vampires (2000) · African Words, African Voices, coedited (2001) · The Assassination of Herbert Chitepo (2003) · Unpopular Sovereignty (2015) · Fighting and Writing (2021)
node.description: Luise White argues that rumour and gossip are historical sources that show how people understood and disputed colonial power. In Speaking with Vampires: Rumor and History in Colonial Africa (2000), she reads their changing details alongside written records, treating contradictions as evidence rather than simply discarding accounts as false. She seeks historical accuracy without reducing stories to a single explanation. Her earlier The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) treats prostitution as work connected to household economies and urban life. In the AHR’s 2021 reception discussion, Frederick Cooper praised its analysis of social reproduction, while Brad Weiss questioned whether its account of Haya women’s pricing sufficiently explained their migration strategies. White also coedited African Words, African Voices (2001) and later examined sovereignty and war in Rhodesia and Zimbabwe.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the acknowledgments to Speaking with Vampires (2000), White credits Frederick Cooper with encouraging her to preserve the ambiguity of vampire stories and examine colonial relations of power and uncertainty.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary acknowledgment, paragraph beginning This book was written, sentence naming Cooper: he encouraged her to let stories “remain ambiguous.” This is White’s explicit report of methodological advice to this project; it establishes neither supervision nor sole derivation. Cooper’s 2021 AHR comment supplies a separate first-person account of his engagement with her work, without extending this influence claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White uses Hayden White’s analogy between historian and psychiatrist to explain how historians rearrange testimony and authorize interpretations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1, Translating Vampires, paragraph beginning It is with these varieties of vocabularies, sentence beginning Here Hayden White’s analogy; she calls the analogy “useful.” Read surrounding discussion of testimony, recoding and unequal power. Chapter 6, Evidence: Vampire Accusations, paragraph beginning Finding the single and note 52 also engage emplotment. His underlying essays remain unread; this is a specific use, not agreement with every aspect of narrative theory.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White proposes reading Foucault’s History of Sexuality for its account of speech and the management of subjects when interpreting gossip in African history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter 2, Gossip and Respectability, paragraphs beginning In the Western world and According to Foucault, with note 15 citing the 1978 English translation, pp. 23–31. White explicitly proposes an “Africanist reading”; the following paragraph tests the approach against gossip performance. This is a selective methodological resource, not a claim that her book applies Foucault’s entire account of sexuality. Foucault’s original French work (1976) and translation were not independently read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White uses Ginzburg’s attention to clues but questions whether a history derived solely from them is too linear for the invention and recurrence of gossip and rumour.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter 2, Voices and Subjects, paragraph beginning Historicizing rumor and gossip and following paragraph beginning The clues and details, with note 48. The criticism is that clue-derived history may be “more linear” than these forms require. Chapter 6, note 53 explicitly preserves her debt to Ginzburg despite this criticism. Chapter 1, Translating Vampires also examines shared vocabularies in his witchcraft histories. Ginzburg’s works remain unread independently; this is a qualified criticism made by White, not a neutral verdict on his scholarship.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White places her treatment of oral and written evidence alongside Portelli’s The Death of Luigi Trastulli (1991) and The Battle of Valle Giulia (1997), crediting European oral historians with reaching this insight earlier.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1, Sources, paragraph beginning This book attempts to treat oral and written material, and its note 139 beginning Europeanists writing on oral history. The note explicitly names Portelli’s two books in support of the equal yet distinct treatment of these sources. Comparative positioning is documented; no personal contact, supervision or exclusive derivation claimed. Portelli’s books remain unread in this dossier. The note misspells Giulia; the existing graph’s publisher-checked title supplies the standard spelling.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Speaking with Vampires (2000), White argues for using rumour and gossip as historical evidence in their own right, reading oral accounts alongside written sources and treating the negotiation of testimony as part of the evidence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter 1 opening; Truth in Vampires, Truth in Oral History, paragraph beginning But how well can oral historians; Sources, final three paragraphs; How to Read this Book, final paragraph. Read her dispute with neutral-interview prescriptions and her explicit retention of accuracy and chronology. The oral and written are “equal but distinct.” This is a claim about historical method, not verification of the events narrated in rumours. Book beyond selected passages unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home (1990) makes Nairobi women’s sex work, household strategies and economic agency central to African women’s history, as Pamela Scully and Corrie Decker explain in the AHR’s 2021 reappraisal discussion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: AHR discussion: Corrie Decker, 5 January 2021, 12:56 am, paragraphs on economic and political change and classroom reception; Pamela Scully, 5 January 2021, 8:07 am, on women as workers and their historical agency. These are named scholars’ accounts of the book’s argument and teaching reception. Decker also questions its usefulness for her own research ethics questions; praise is not unanimous. The 1990 book is unread in full; no content of individual women’s oral narratives is reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home (1990) connects prostitution to household reproduction and the colonial wage economy, an intervention Frederick Cooper appraises in the AHR’s 2021 reappraisal discussion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: AHR discussion: complete Fred Cooper contribution, 5 January 2021, 6:31 pm, especially paragraphs beginning For all her engagement and Her book made a splash. Cooper identifies political economy, social reproduction and the changing colonial state as specific arguments, and recalls publishing a precursor in Struggle for the City (1983). This is an attributed substantive reading of White’s book, not an independent reading of the book or its 1983 precursor.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) contributed to gender history by situating sexuality within economic and political change, as Corrie Decker explains in the AHR's 2021 reception discussion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Decker explicitly names the field contribution and explains its argument. This is substantive retrospective reception, not a contributor credit. Original book unread in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Comforts of Home: Prostitution in Colonial Nairobi (1990) contributed to African urban history by showing cities as places of enjoyment and social experimentation, as Paul Ocobock explains in the AHR's 2021 reception discussion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ocobock identifies a specific change in urban interpretation. Maddox's publisher extract independently identifies White's pioneering place in East African urban history, without naming a particular White title.
